\\mathcal{L}: The loss: the single number training tries to make as small as possible. Lower means the model fits the data and respects the extra terms better.
L: The loss: the single number training tries to make as small as possible.
\\lambda: Penalty weight: how strongly the added term counts against the main objective. A larger value enforces that term harder, at some cost in fit.
\\theta: The model's trainable parameters (its weights), the things training adjusts.
y: The true outcome the model is trained to predict: a label such as 1 for positive and 0 for negative, or a measured value.
p: The model's predicted probability that the outcome is positive (between 0 and 1).
\\hat{p}: The model's estimated probability, after calibration where one is applied.
x: The input features describing one example (what the model sees).
X: The matrix of input features for all examples.
Y: The observed outcome for a group of units, such as the average result in a treatment or control group.
w: A weight that scales how much a particular example, class or term counts in the loss.
t: Time step, or token position in a text sequence.
e: Euler's number (about 2.718), the base of the exponential function.
\\sum: Sum: add up the term for every value of the index written under it (all examples, time steps, classes and so on).
\\prod: Product: multiply the term over every value of the index written under it.
\\int: Integral: add up a continuously varying quantity over the range shown.
\\log: Natural logarithm. It turns probabilities into log-likelihood terms that add up and punish confident mistakes heavily.
\\exp: Exponential function: e raised to the power shown.
\\mid: 'Given': what follows is the information the probability or prediction is conditioned on.
\\frac: Fraction: the top part divided by the bottom part.
\\|: Norm: the length of a vector. The squared norm of a difference is the sum of squared errors.
\\max: Maximum: pick the value of the variable written under it that gives the largest result (or, written alone, the larger of the listed values).
\\min: Minimum: pick the value of the variable written under it that gives the smallest result (or, written alone, the smaller of the listed values).
\\arg: The argument that achieves the optimum: the setting of the variable below it that gives the best result.
\\mathbb{E}: Expectation: the average over everything that could happen, weighted by how likely it is.
\\mathbb{1}: Indicator: equals 1 when the condition in the brackets is true and 0 otherwise.
\\Pr: Probability of the event written inside the brackets.
\\mu: The model's predicted mean (expected value) of the outcome.
\\hat{\\mu}: The model's estimated mean (expected value) of the outcome.
\\sigma: Standard deviation: the model's predicted spread, or uncertainty, around its mean prediction.
\\rho: Pinball (quantile) loss: penalises under-prediction and over-prediction by different amounts so the model learns a chosen percentile instead of the average.
q: Quantile level between 0 and 1, for example 0.9 for the 90th percentile.
\\hat{q}: The model's predicted value at the chosen quantile.
\\gamma: Discount factor between 0 and 1: how much a reward one step later is worth compared with the same reward now.
\\alpha: Intercept: the baseline level of the outcome before any predictor is added.
\\beta: Coefficient: how much the outcome changes per unit of the predictor it multiplies.
\\pi: The policy: the rule that chooses an action in each situation.
\\tau: Temperature: scales similarity scores before the softmax; a smaller value makes the model sharper and more confident.
\\hat{\\tau}: The estimated treatment effect (uplift): how much the treatment changes the outcome for this unit or group.
\\varepsilon: Random noise: the part of the outcome the model does not explain.
\\epsilon: Random noise or a small tolerance.
\\Delta: A change or difference in the quantity that follows.
\\kappa: A tuning constant that scales the term it multiplies.
\\Phi: The cumulative distribution function of the normal distribution.
\\phi: A learned feature map or embedding function.
\\Sigma: Covariance matrix: how the uncertainties of different quantities vary together.
\\top: Transpose: flips a vector or matrix so that a dot product can be taken.
\\mathrm{BCE}: Binary cross-entropy: the standard loss for yes/no predictions. It is large when the model gives a low probability to what actually happened.
\\mathrm{CE}: Cross-entropy for multi-class labels: large when the model gives a low probability to the true class.
\\mathrm{FL}: Focal loss: cross-entropy that down-weights easy examples so that rare, hard positives drive learning.
\\mathrm{Huber}: Huber loss: squared error for small mistakes and absolute error for large ones, so outliers do not dominate training.
\\mathrm{SmoothL1}: Smooth L1 loss: like Huber loss, gentle on small errors and linear on large ones.
\\mathrm{MSE}: Mean squared error: the average of squared differences between prediction and truth.
\\mathrm{KL}: Kullback-Leibler divergence: how far one probability distribution is from another (zero when they are identical).
\\mathrm{Calibration}: Calibration penalty: grows when predicted probabilities disagree with observed frequencies, for example predictions of 30% that come true 20% of the time.
\\mathrm{ECE}: Expected calibration error: the average gap between predicted probability and observed frequency across probability bins.
\\mathrm{Brier}: Brier score: the mean squared difference between predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome.
\\mathrm{RankLoss}: Ranking loss: penalises placing a less relevant item above a more relevant one.
\\mathrm{GraphReg}: Graph regulariser: a penalty that pushes connected nodes to have similar representations.
\\mathrm{InfoNCE}: Contrastive loss that pulls true matching pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart.
\\mathrm{Contrastive}: Contrastive loss: pulls similar items together and pushes dissimilar items apart in embedding space.
\\mathrm{SupCon}: Supervised contrastive loss: pulls together all items that share a label and pushes apart the rest.
\\mathrm{Triplet}: Triplet loss: requires an anchor to be closer to a matching example than to a non-matching one by a margin.
\\mathrm{TripletLoss}: Triplet loss: requires an anchor to be closer to a matching example than to a non-matching one by a margin.
\\mathrm{BPR}: Bayesian personalised ranking loss: trains the model to score items a user chose above items they did not.
\\mathrm{OrdinalCE}: Ordinal cross-entropy: cross-entropy that treats classes as ordered, so predicting far from the true grade costs more than predicting next to it.
\\mathrm{Ordinal}: An ordinal loss: penalises predictions by how far they fall from the true ordered grade.
\\mathrm{ZILN}: Zero-inflated log-normal loss: models outcomes that are often exactly zero and otherwise positive with a long right tail, such as customer spend.
\\mathrm{Dec}: The decoder: the network part that rebuilds the input from its compressed code.
\\mathrm{Enc}: The encoder: the network part that compresses the input into a short code.
\\mathrm{PSI}: Population stability index: a measure of how much a feature's distribution has drifted from its reference.
\\mathrm{Tweedie}: Tweedie deviance: a loss for non-negative outcomes with many zeros and a heavy right tail, such as insurance claims.
\\mathrm{PoissonDeviance}: Poisson deviance: a loss for count outcomes that measures how far predicted rates are from observed counts.
\\mathrm{Deviance}: Deviance: a likelihood-based loss that measures how far predictions are from the observed outcomes.
\\mathrm{Dice}: Dice loss: one minus the overlap between the predicted and true regions, used for segmentation.
\\mathrm{NDCG}: Normalised discounted cumulative gain: a ranking quality score that rewards relevant items near the top of the list.
\\mathrm{MMD}: Maximum mean discrepancy: a measure of how different two distributions are.
\\mathrm{IPM}: Integral probability metric: a distance between two distributions, used to make treated and control groups look alike.
\\mathrm{Cov}: Covariance: how two quantities vary together.
\\mathrm{Var}: Variance: how widely a quantity varies around its mean.
\\mathrm{Hill}: Hill function: an S-shaped saturation curve in which each extra unit of spend adds less.
\\mathrm{Adstock}: Adstock: the lagged, decaying effect of past advertising on later periods.
\\mathrm{ListNet}: ListNet loss: trains a model to reproduce the whole ranked list by matching probability distributions over rankings.
\\mathrm{GroupDRO}: Group distributionally robust objective: minimises the loss of the worst-performing group instead of the average.
\\mathrm{EqualisedOdds}: Equalised odds penalty: grows when true-positive and false-positive rates differ between groups.
\\mathrm{DemographicParity}: Demographic parity penalty: grows when positive prediction rates differ between groups.
\\mathrm{Haversine}: Haversine distance: the great-circle distance between two latitude and longitude points.
\\mathrm{KMeans}: K-means objective: the squared distance from each point to its cluster centre.
\\mathrm{Survival}: Survival loss: a likelihood that handles customers or units still active at the end of observation (censored).
\\mathrm{Poisson}: Poisson likelihood: a probability model for counts of events.
\\mathrm{LogNormal}: Log-normal likelihood: a probability model for positive values whose logarithm is normally distributed.
\\mathrm{Evidential}: Evidential loss: trains the model to output its own uncertainty along with each prediction.
\\hat{r}: The model's predicted value of the quantity r.
\\hat{x}: The reconstruction of the input x produced by the decoder.
\\hat{\\lambda}: The estimated rate (how often the event occurs per unit time).
\\hat{b}: The model's estimated value of b.
\\bar{Y}: The average outcome of the group named in the subscript.
\\bar{X}: The average of the covariate X.
\\tilde{Y}: The outcome after removing the part explained by the other covariates (a residual).
\\tilde{T}: The treatment assignment after removing the part explained by the other covariates (a residual).
y_{<t}: All tokens before position t: the text the model has already read or generated.
p_\\theta: The language model's probability of the next token y_t, given the earlier tokens and the context written after the bar.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{det}}: Detection loss: how well objects are found and their boxes placed.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{seg}}: Segmentation loss: how well the region of interest is outlined pixel by pixel.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{segmentation}}: Segmentation loss: how well the region of interest is outlined pixel by pixel.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{cls}}: Classification loss: how well each detected item is given the right class.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{CTC}}: Connectionist temporal classification loss: aligns a signal such as audio or a line image with its text without frame-by-frame labels.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{BCE}}: Binary cross-entropy part of the loss, for yes/no predictions.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{focal}}: Focal loss part of the loss: cross-entropy that concentrates on hard, rare examples.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{perceptual}}: Perceptual loss: how different the output looks to a vision network compared with the target image.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{adv}}: Adversarial loss: trains the generator to produce images a discriminator cannot tell from real ones.
\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{recon}}: Reconstruction loss: how well the model rebuilds a normal image, so defects show up as large errors.
\\mathrm{Pinball}: Pinball (quantile) loss: penalises under- and over-prediction asymmetrically so the output is a chosen quantile, such as the 90th percentile, rather than the average.
